about: The first of these prayers is all but a quotation from the book of Daniel (3:39–40), which reads the two phrases the other way round: “in a contrite heart and a spirit of humility may we be received”. It is the prayer of the three young men in the furnace — men with no sacrifice left to offer, the temple being destroyed, and so they offer themselves. At the altar, where the offering already lies on the corporal, the priest asks in those same words that he and those he offers for be the ones received: “suscipiámur” — may we be received, not “may it be received”. The second prayer is the only one in the whole offertory that calls: come.

s01.narrative: The priest sets the chalice on the corporal and covers it with the pall. Bowed a little, his joined hands resting on the altar, he goes on.

s02.translation: In a spirit of humility and a contrite heart may we be received by Thee, Lord: and so let our sacrifice be made this day in Thy sight, that it may please Thee, Lord God.

s03.narrative: The priest stands upright, spreads his hands and raises them, lifts his eyes to heaven for a moment and at once lowers them.

s05.narrative: The priest blesses host and chalice together with the sign of the cross, and finishes the prayer.

s06.translation: and bless this sacrifice, prepared for Thy holy name.

w003.function: A genitive where an adjective would stand in English, as throughout the psalter: a spirit of humility for “a humble spirit”.

w007.function: Agrees with “ánimo” (w006). Contérere is to grind to powder — a contrite heart is a crushed one, not merely a sorry one.

w008.function: Passive, first person plural: what is asked to be received is us, not the gifts. The same verb as the “Súscipe” of the prayer over the host.

w010.function: Ablative of the agent after “a” (w009): by whom we are to be received.

w014.function: Fio serves Latin as the passive of fácere: “let it be done” is at once “let it be made”.

w020.function: One word fastens the prayer to the day in hand: not sacrifice in general but today's.

w023.function: Dative after “pláceat” (w022): placére governs the dative of the person.

w025.function: A second address, this time doubled — each of the prayer's two petitions ends on an address.

w026.function: The one call in the whole offertory that asks God to come.

w027.function: A noun in -tor names the doer of an action: the one who sanctifies. Its vocative is the same as its nominative.

w030.function: The same three words that close the address in the prayer over the host — there after “sancte Pater”, here after “sanctificátor”.

w032.function: Bene-dícere: to speak well of a thing, and by that to hallow it.

w033.function: Agrees with “sacrifícium” (w034); it points at what lies on the corporal.

w037.function: A dative of advantage with “præparátum” (w038): made ready for thy name.

w038.function: Agrees with “sacrifícium” (w034): the sacrifice already made ready, and only now blessed.
